title: Mutual Fund: Specialized Investment Fund Distributors
blurb: The common certification for mutual fund and SIF distributors: fund basics, the SIF framework, plus equity and interest rate derivatives.

units.title: Investment landscape, mutual fund concept and structure
units.overview: Asset classes, risk and return, how a mutual fund pools money and the sponsor-trustee-AMC structure.
facts: Risk and return
Higher expected return generally needs higher risk, and investors are compensated for bearing risk that cannot be diversified away.
A client who wants high returns is told to expect bigger falls too.
A high return can be earned with no added risk.
Inflation and real return
Real return is the return after adjusting for inflation, so it shows the rise in purchasing power.
An 8% return with 6% inflation gives roughly 2% real return.
Nominal return already shows purchasing power.
Mutual fund
A mutual fund pools money from many investors and invests it in securities according to a stated objective, managed by professionals.
Thousands of investors share one diversified portfolio.
A mutual fund guarantees a fixed return to investors.
Unit holders and units
Investors own units of a scheme in proportion to their money invested, and share its gains, losses and expenses.
An investor holding 1% of a scheme's units owns 1% of its portfolio.
Unit holders own a specific share held by the fund.
Three-tier structure
A mutual fund has a sponsor, a trust with trustees and an asset management company, with a custodian holding the securities.
The trustees oversee the AMC which manages the schemes.
The AMC owns the fund assets in its own name.
Role of trustees
Trustees are responsible for protecting unit holders' interests and for overseeing the AMC's compliance.
Trustees review the AMC's reports every quarter.
Trustees pick the stocks for each scheme.
Role of custodian
A custodian holds the scheme's securities in safe custody and settles transactions, separate from the AMC.
Securities of a scheme are kept with an independent custodian.
The AMC holds securities in its own accounts.
Advantages of mutual funds
Funds give diversification, professional management, liquidity, affordability and transparency in one product.
An investor with small savings holds dozens of stocks through one fund.
Funds remove all investment risk.
Open-ended and closed-ended
Open-ended schemes accept entries and exits at NAV on any business day, while closed-ended schemes have a fixed maturity and are listed.
An investor redeems an open-ended scheme at that day's NAV.
Closed-ended schemes can be redeemed from the AMC any day.

units.title: Legal, regulatory framework and scheme information
units.overview: SEBI regulation, the role of AMFI, scheme documents, offer rules and scheme categories.
facts: SEBI as regulator
SEBI regulates mutual funds in India through the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations and issues circulars to AMCs, trustees and distributors.
SEBI changes how schemes are categorised through a circular.
Each AMC makes its own rules without SEBI's approval.
AMFI
AMFI is the industry body of AMCs that promotes standards, sets code of conduct for distributors and registers them with an ARN.
A distributor gets an ARN code through AMFI.
AMFI is the statutory regulator of mutual funds.
ARN and EUIN
A distributor needs an AMFI Registration Number to sell funds, and an EUIN identifies the employee or sales person who gave advice.
A bank staff member quotes an EUIN on the application form.
A distributor can sell funds without an ARN.
Scheme Information Document
The SID contains the scheme's objective, strategy, risks, fees and other details an investor needs before investing.
An investor reads the SID before applying in an NFO.
The SID is optional and not available to investors.
Statement of Additional Information
The SAI has details about the mutual fund such as constitution, trustees and legal matters, and is common to all its schemes.
A distributor checks the SAI for the sponsor details.
The SAI is specific to one scheme only.
Key Information Memorandum
The KIM is a short summary of key scheme features that is given with the application form.
An applicant receives the KIM along with the form.
The KIM replaces the SID for risk factors.
Scheme categorisation
SEBI groups schemes into categories such as equity, debt, hybrid, solution-oriented and others, with defined features for each.
Large cap, mid cap and flexi cap are equity categories.
AMCs can name categories freely.
One scheme per category
An AMC can generally offer only one scheme in each defined category, with a few exceptions, to avoid confusion.
An AMC cannot launch two large cap funds.
An AMC can launch any number of schemes in a category.
Riskometer
The riskometer shows a scheme's risk on six levels from low to very high and must be shown on scheme documents.
A cover page shows a dial at very high.
The riskometer shows expected return.
New fund offer
An NFO is the first-time offer of units of a new scheme, usually at a face value of ₹10 per unit.
An investor applies for units of a new scheme at ₹10.
NFO units are priced at the earlier NAV of another scheme.

units.title: Distribution, NAV, expenses and tax
units.overview: How funds are sold, how NAV and TER work and how mutual fund income is taxed.
facts: Net asset value
NAV is the net assets of a scheme after liabilities divided by units outstanding, and is the price at which units are bought and sold.
A scheme with ₹100 crore net assets and 5 crore units has a NAV of ₹20.
NAV is the market price set by supply and demand.
Total expense ratio
TER is the annual cost of running a scheme as a percentage of assets, charged to the scheme and reflected in NAV.
A 1% TER reduces the return the investor sees by 1% a year.
TER is paid by the investor separately at purchase.
Direct and regular plans
A direct plan has no distributor commission and a lower TER, while a regular plan includes distributor commission in its expenses.
A client buying through a distributor holds the regular plan.
A direct plan costs more than a regular plan.
Exit load
Exit load is a charge deducted on redemption within a stated period and goes to the scheme, reducing the amount the investor receives.
A 1% exit load on redemption within one year reduces the proceeds.
Exit load is charged on all units regardless of holding period.
Cut-off time
Applications for liquid funds and others are allotted the NAV of the day only if received before the cut-off time, otherwise the next day's NAV applies.
A purchase after the cut-off time gets the next day's NAV.
Any time of the day gets the same day's NAV.
Stamp duty on units
Stamp duty is charged at 0.005% on purchase of units, including switches and SIP instalments.
A small deduction appears at allotment.
Stamp duty is charged only on redemption.
Equity fund taxation
Gains on equity-oriented funds are short-term if sold within 12 months, taxed at 20%, and long-term above that, taxed at 12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh in a year (as at writing).
An investor with ₹3 lakh long-term gain pays tax on the amount above ₹1.25 lakh.
Equity fund gains are tax-free.
Taxation depends on portfolio
How a fund is taxed depends on the nature of its underlying portfolio, so distributors must check the scheme's tax treatment from its documents before advising.
A distributor checks how the scheme is classified for tax.
All schemes are taxed alike.
Distributor commission
AMCs pay trail commission to distributors for regular plans and this must be disclosed to investors.
A distributor tells the client how she is paid.
Commission is hidden from the investor.

units.title: Investor services, risk, performance and scheme selection
units.overview: Account services, KYC, risk profiling, performance measures and choosing a scheme.
facts: KYC
Investors must complete KYC with proof of identity and address and PAN before investing in funds.
A first-time investor completes KYC before investing.
KYC is only needed above ₹50,000 and only for equity funds.
Systematic investment plan
A SIP invests a fixed amount at regular intervals, averaging cost across market ups and downs.
An investor puts ₹5,000 every month.
A SIP guarantees profits.
Systematic withdrawal plan
A SWP lets an investor take a fixed amount at regular intervals by redeeming units.
A retiree withdraws ₹20,000 every month.
A SWP puts money into the scheme monthly.
Systematic transfer plan
A STP moves a fixed amount at regular intervals from one scheme to another.
An investor moves ₹10,000 monthly from a liquid fund to an equity fund.
A STP withdraws money to the bank.
Standard deviation
Standard deviation measures how much returns vary around their average, so a higher value means a more volatile fund.
A fund with 18% standard deviation swings more than one with 8%.
A higher standard deviation means safer returns.
Beta
Beta measures a fund's sensitivity to the market, where 1.2 means a move 20% larger than the market.
A fund with beta 1.2 rises 12% when the market rises 10%.
Beta is the fund's absolute return.
Sharpe ratio
The Sharpe ratio measures excess return over the risk-free rate per unit of total risk.
A higher Sharpe ratio means better risk-adjusted performance.
A lower Sharpe ratio means better risk-adjusted performance.
CAGR
CAGR is the annualised rate at which an investment grows over a period longer than a year.
₹100 growing to ₹121 in two years is a 10% CAGR.
CAGR is the simple total gain divided by years.
Benchmark and tracking
A fund's performance should be compared with its stated benchmark over comparable periods and consistently, not for one period only.
An adviser compares a fund with its benchmark over five years.
A fund can be judged by its last month's return.
Risk profiling
Risk profiling assesses a client's capacity and willingness to take risk to guide product choice.
A distributor asks how the client would feel if the portfolio fell 25%.
Every client of the same age has the same risk profile.
Suitability
A distributor must recommend products that suit the client's goals, horizon, risk profile and financial situation.
A conservative client is not pushed into a high-risk fund.
The highest commission product is the suitable one.

units.title: Specialized Investment Funds: framework and rules
units.overview: What a SIF is, how it sits between mutual funds and PMS, the strategies, the ₹10 lakh threshold, limits and distributor duties.
facts: Specialized Investment Fund
A SIF is a SEBI-regulated investment product launched by an AMC for investors who want more sophisticated strategies than regular mutual funds, with a higher minimum investment.
A wealthy investor wants a long-short strategy not available in ordinary funds.
A SIF is the same as a regular mutual fund scheme.
Position between MF and PMS
SIFs sit between mutual funds and portfolio management services, with MF-style pooling and regulation but more flexible strategies.
A client wants more flexibility than a fund but not a customised PMS.
SIFs are an individually managed portfolio for each investor.
Minimum investment
The minimum investment in SIFs is ₹10 lakh per investor, aggregated across all the SIF strategies of the same AMC at the PAN level.
An investor's investments across two strategies of one AMC are added up for the ₹10 lakh test.
The minimum ₹10 lakh applies separately to each strategy.
Accredited investors
Accredited investors are exempt from the ₹10 lakh minimum investment.
An accredited investor invests a smaller amount in a SIF.
Accredited investors must invest ₹1 crore.
Passive breach of minimum
If market movement reduces an investor's holding below ₹10 lakh, the investor can only redeem the entire remaining amount rather than part.
An investor's holding falls to ₹9 lakh because of NAV decline.
Falling below ₹10 lakh makes the folio freeze permanently.
SIP, SWP and STP in SIFs
SIPs, SWPs and STPs are allowed in SIFs provided the investor's investment meets the minimum threshold.
An investor with ₹10 lakh sets up a SIP into a SIF.
SIFs allow only lump sum investment.
Equity Long-Short
The Equity Long-Short strategy must invest at least 80% in equity and equity-related instruments and may take limited short positions through derivatives.
A SIF buys stocks and also shorts through index futures.
Equity Long-Short can invest only in debt.
Equity Ex-Top 100 Long-Short
This strategy must invest at least 65% in equity of companies outside the top 100 by market capitalisation.
A SIF holds mostly mid and small caps outside the largest 100.
This strategy must invest only in the top 100 stocks.
Sector Rotation Long-Short
This equity strategy must keep at least 80% in equity and can be exposed to a maximum of four sectors at a time.
A SIF shifts between banking, auto, IT and pharma.
Sector Rotation must be spread equally across ten sectors.
Debt Long-Short
The Debt Long-Short strategy can take up to 25% unhedged short exposure through exchange-traded debt derivatives.
A debt SIF shorts interest rate futures when it expects yields to rise.
Debt SIFs cannot use any derivatives.
Sectoral Debt Long-Short
This strategy invests in at least two sectors, with no more than 75% in a single sector and up to 25% unhedged short exposure.
A debt SIF holds 70% in one sector and the rest elsewhere.
This strategy can put 100% in one sector.
Hybrid Long-Short
The Hybrid Long-Short strategy holds at least 25% each in equity and debt, with maximum 25% short exposure through unhedged derivatives.
A hybrid SIF keeps 40% in equity and 40% in debt.
A Hybrid Long-Short fund must be fully invested in equity.
Derivative and short limits
Unhedged short exposure through derivatives is limited to 25% of net assets, and non-hedging use of exchange-traded derivatives is also limited to 25%.
A SIF cannot run an unhedged short of 40% of net assets.
SIFs have no limit on unhedged short positions.
Gross exposure cap
Cumulative gross exposure across cash and derivatives must not exceed 100% of net assets.
A SIF cannot leverage beyond its net assets.
SIFs can freely leverage to two times net assets.
Redemption and structure
SIFs can be open-ended or interval and redemption notice can be up to 15 working days, with the redemption frequency set out in the scheme documents.
A SIF allows redemption only at fixed intervals.
All SIFs allow instant daily redemption.
Separate branding
SIFs must keep branding and marketing distinct from the mutual fund, with the MF brand shown only as the offeror and not more prominently than the SIF brand.
A SIF advertisement uses a smaller MF brand name than the SIF name.
A SIF must use the MF brand more prominently.
Risks of SIFs
SIFs carry market, strategy, derivative, liquidity and concentration risks and do not guarantee returns or capital.
A distributor explains that short positions can lose money.
SIFs protect the investor's capital.
Suitability for SIFs
SIFs suit investors who understand complex strategies, can bear higher risk, accept lower liquidity and have a higher net worth, so suitability must be checked before sale.
A distributor declines to sell a SIF to an investor who needs liquidity every month.
SIFs are suitable for any retail investor.

units.title: Basics of derivatives and understanding index
units.overview: What derivatives are, who uses them, the types of contracts and how stock indices are built.
facts: Derivative
A derivative is a contract whose value is derived from an underlying asset such as a share, index, currency or interest rate.
An index future derives its value from the index.
A derivative has a value independent of any underlying.
Hedger
A hedger uses derivatives to reduce an existing risk.
A fund holding shares sells index futures to protect against a fall.
A hedger takes derivative positions to increase risk.
Speculator
A speculator takes a view on price movements and accepts risk in hope of profit.
A trader buys futures expecting the index to rise.
A speculator uses derivatives to remove risk.
Arbitrageur
An arbitrageur exploits price differences between related markets to earn riskless profit.
A trader buys in the cash market and sells in the futures market when they are mispriced.
An arbitrageur depends on the market direction.
Types of derivatives
The main types are forwards, futures, options and swaps.
A fund uses futures and options on an index.
Shares and bonds are derivatives.
Exchange-traded and OTC
Exchange-traded derivatives are standardised and cleared through a clearing corporation, while OTC derivatives are customised and privately negotiated.
Index futures trade on an exchange.
OTC derivatives are traded on exchange with standard terms.
Underlying
The underlying is the asset, rate or index from which the derivative gets its value.
An option on the Nifty has the Nifty index as the underlying.
The underlying is the derivative contract itself.
Stock index
A stock index measures the value of a basket of shares to show the market's movement.
The Nifty 50 tracks 50 large stocks.
An index tracks a single stock.
Free-float market capitalisation
Index weights are commonly based on free-float market capitalisation, which counts only the shares available for public trading.
A company with a large promoter holding gets a lower weight than its full market cap.
Free-float counts shares held by promoters.
Index uses
Indices are used as benchmarks, for index funds and ETFs and as the underlying for futures and options.
A fund compares itself with its benchmark index.
Indices cannot be used for investing.
Systematic and unsystematic risk
Systematic risk affects the whole market and cannot be diversified away, while unsystematic risk is specific to a company and can be diversified.
An index future hedges market risk.
Index futures hedge company-specific risk completely.

units.title: Forwards and futures
units.overview: Futures contracts, pricing, margins, mark-to-market and settlement.
facts: Forward contract
A forward is a customised OTC agreement to buy or sell an asset at a fixed price on a future date.
Two parties agree today on the price of an asset for delivery in three months.
A forward is traded on the exchange with fixed terms.
Futures contract
A futures contract is a standardised exchange-traded agreement to buy or sell an underlying at a set price on a future date.
An investor buys the near-month index future.
Futures contracts are customised for each buyer.
Long and short futures
A long position gains when the price rises, and a short position gains when the price falls.
An investor who sells a future profits if the index falls.
A short futures position gains when the price rises.
Lot size
Futures and options trade in fixed lots, so the contract value is the price multiplied by the lot size.
A future at 20,000 with lot size 50 has a contract value of ₹10 lakh.
One can trade a single unit of a futures contract.
Cost of carry
A futures price is the spot price plus the cost of carrying the asset to the future date, so futures normally trade above spot in the usual case.
A one-month future trades above spot due to financing cost.
Futures always trade below the spot price.
Basis
Basis is the difference between the spot price and the futures price, and it narrows to zero at expiry.
The gap between spot and futures falls as expiry nears.
Basis widens as expiry nears.
Initial margin
Initial margin is the deposit a trader must put up to open a futures position, to cover potential losses.
A trader deposits margin before buying an index future.
Initial margin is the full contract value.
Mark-to-market
Futures positions are marked to market daily, with gains and losses settled each day through the margin account.
A fall in price leads to a daily debit to the long holder.
Gains and losses are settled only at expiry.
Margin call
If the margin balance falls below the maintenance level, the trader gets a margin call to top it up.
A client gets a call to add funds after a loss.
A margin call returns excess margin to the trader.
Cash settlement of index futures
Index futures are settled in cash at expiry, as the index cannot be delivered.
On expiry, the difference is paid in cash.
Index futures are settled by delivering all index shares.
Hedging with index futures
A fund can protect a diversified equity portfolio by selling index futures, reducing market risk while keeping the portfolio.
A fund sells Nifty futures to hedge a fall.
Selling index futures increases exposure to a market fall.
Futures P&L
The profit on a long futures trade is the exit price minus entry price multiplied by lot size and lots.
Buy at 100 and sell at 110 with a lot of 100 gives ₹1,000.
The profit on a long trade is the entry minus exit price.
Clearing corporation
A clearing corporation becomes the counterparty to both sides of every exchange-traded contract, reducing counterparty risk.
A trader need not worry about the other side defaulting.
Each trader faces the counterparty's default risk directly.

units.title: Options
units.overview: Calls, puts, premium, moneyness, payoffs, pricing drivers and Greeks.
facts: Call option
A call option gives the buyer the right, not the obligation, to buy the underlying at the strike price.
A buyer pays premium for the right to buy at 100.
A call option gives the buyer the right to sell.
Put option
A put option gives the buyer the right, not the obligation, to sell the underlying at the strike price.
A holder buys a put to protect a falling portfolio.
A put option gives the buyer the obligation to sell.
Option premium
The premium is the price paid by the buyer to the seller of the option and is the buyer's maximum loss.
A buyer pays ₹50 per unit and can lose at most that.
The buyer of an option can lose more than the premium.
Writer's risk
The option seller earns the premium but can face large or unlimited loss, so must keep margin.
A call writer loses if the price rises sharply.
An option writer's loss is limited to the premium.
Strike price
The strike is the fixed price at which the option holder can buy or sell the underlying.
A call with a strike of 18,000 on the index.
The strike changes every day.
European and American
A European option can be exercised only at expiry while an American option can be exercised any time before expiry, and index options in India are European.
Nifty options are exercised at expiry.
Index options in India are American.
Moneyness
A call is in the money when spot is above strike, at the money when equal and out of the money when below, and the reverse for a put.
A call with strike 90 when spot is 100 is in the money.
A call is in the money when spot is below strike.
Intrinsic and time value
Premium equals intrinsic value plus time value, and time value falls to zero at expiry.
An in-the-money option has intrinsic value plus time value.
An out-of-the-money option has intrinsic value.
Long call payoff
A long call's profit at expiry is the greater of spot minus strike and zero, less the premium.
Strike 100, spot 120, premium 5 gives a profit of 15.
A long call's profit is limited to the premium.
Breakeven
The breakeven for a long call is the strike plus premium, and for a long put it is the strike minus premium.
A call at strike 100 and premium 5 breaks even at 105.
The breakeven of a long call is strike minus premium.
Delta
Delta shows how much the option price changes for a unit move in the underlying.
A call delta of 0.5 gains about 0.5 for each 1 rise.
Delta measures time decay.
Theta
Theta shows the loss of option value as time passes, hurting option buyers.
An option loses value each day while spot is unchanged.
Theta benefits option buyers as time passes.
Vega
Vega measures the sensitivity of an option's price to changes in volatility, and higher volatility increases option prices.
An option gains when volatility rises.
Higher volatility reduces the value of all options.
Put-call parity
Put-call parity links call, put, spot and the present value of strike for European options with the same strike and expiry.
Mispricing between a call and put creates an arbitrage chance.
Put and call prices are independent of each other.

units.title: Strategies using equity futures and options
units.overview: Hedging, spreads, straddles and how funds and SIFs use equity derivatives.
facts: Protective put
A protective put is buying a put against shares held, which limits the downside while keeping the upside.
An investor holds shares and buys a put at a lower strike.
A protective put involves selling a put.
Covered call
A covered call is holding shares and selling a call, earning premium but capping the upside.
A fund sells a call on shares it holds.
A covered call has no limit to the loss.
Long straddle
A long straddle buys a call and a put at the same strike and expiry, gaining from a big move in either direction.
A trader expects a large move after results.
A long straddle gains when the price stays still.
Bull call spread
A bull call spread buys a lower strike call and sells a higher strike call, giving limited profit and limited loss.
A trader mildly expects a rise.
A bull call spread has unlimited profit.
Bear put spread
A bear put spread buys a higher strike put and sells a lower strike put to profit from a moderate fall.
A trader mildly expects a fall.
A bear put spread profits from a rise.
Long-short use
A long-short equity fund buys stocks expected to rise and uses futures or options to short those expected to fall, reducing market exposure.
A SIF is long on strong stocks and short on index futures.
A long-short strategy is always fully long.
Short futures to hedge
Selling futures against a stock portfolio offsets losses on the portfolio if the market falls, though it gives up gains on a rise.
A fund sells futures before an uncertain event.
Short futures add to losses when the market falls.
Arbitrage use
Equity arbitrage funds exploit price differences between cash and futures markets, with the futures sold against the shares bought.
A fund buys shares and sells futures to lock the spread.
Arbitrage funds take full directional equity risk.
Derivative risk
Leverage in derivatives magnifies both gains and losses, so position limits and margins matter.
A small market move causes a large margin loss.
Derivatives lower risk in every use.

units.title: Interest rates, fixed income markets and interest rate derivatives
units.overview: Interest rate basics, bond price and yield, and why interest rate derivatives exist.
facts: Bond price and yield
Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions, so a rise in yields lowers bond prices.
A bond falls in price when yields rise.
Bond prices rise when yields rise.
Coupon
A coupon is the periodic interest payment a bond pays based on its face value and coupon rate.
A 7% bond of ₹100 pays ₹7 a year.
A coupon is the bond's market price.
Yield to maturity
Yield to maturity is the return from holding a bond to maturity, with all coupons reinvested at the same rate.
An investor compares bonds by their yields.
Yield to maturity ignores the bond's price.
Government securities
G-Secs are issued by the government and have no credit risk, but they carry interest rate risk.
A 10-year G-Sec falls in value if yields rise.
G-Secs have no interest rate risk.
Duration
Duration measures a bond's sensitivity to interest rate changes, and a longer duration means greater price change for a change in yield.
A bond with a duration of 7 moves more than one with 2.
Duration measures a bond's credit risk.
Interest rate risk
Interest rate risk is the risk that the value of a bond or fund changes because rates change.
A debt fund falls when yields rise.
Interest rate risk is the same as default risk.
Interest rate derivative
An interest rate derivative is a contract whose value depends on an interest rate or a bond price, and it is used to hedge or take a view on rates.
A debt fund hedges a rate rise with a futures contract.
Interest rate derivatives depend on equity prices.
Money market
The money market deals in short-term instruments such as T-bills, commercial paper and call money.
A liquid fund holds T-bills.
The money market deals only in long-term bonds.

units.title: Interest rate futures and options
units.overview: How exchange-traded interest rate futures and options are built, priced and settled.
facts: Interest rate futures
An interest rate future is an exchange-traded contract on an underlying interest rate instrument, such as a government security or T-bill.
A fund buys a G-Sec future on the exchange.
Interest rate futures trade only over the counter.
Notional underlying
Interest rate futures on bonds use a notional security, so settlement is in cash and no actual bond is delivered.
A contract settles in cash against a notional bond.
The seller must deliver a bond at expiry.
Price and yield
The futures price moves inversely to yield, so a rise in yields lowers the futures price.
A long position loses if yields rise.
A long position gains when yields rise.
Long and short IRF
A long position gains when yields fall and a short position gains when yields rise.
A bond fund sells futures to hedge against a rate rise.
A short position gains when yields fall.
PV01
PV01 is the change in the value of a position for a one basis point change in yield.
A position loses ₹5,000 for each 1 bp rise in yield.
PV01 is measured for a 1% change in price.
Basis point
One basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point, so 100 basis points equal 1%.
A rise from 7.00% to 7.25% is 25 basis points.
One basis point equals one percent.
Hedge ratio
The hedge ratio gives the number of futures contracts needed to offset the portfolio's interest rate sensitivity, using the PV01 of the portfolio and the future.
A fund divides its portfolio PV01 by the future's PV01.
The hedge ratio is the portfolio's credit rating.
T-bill futures
A T-bill future is based on a short-term treasury bill and can be used to hedge short-term rates.
A short-term fund hedges using T-bill futures.
T-bill futures are based on long-term bonds.
Mark-to-market in IRF
Interest rate futures are marked to market daily like other futures, with gains and losses settled through margin.
A day's yield rise is settled in the margin account.
Interest rate futures are settled only at expiry.
Interest rate options
An interest rate option gives the buyer the right, not the obligation, to buy or sell the underlying interest rate instrument at a strike.
A buyer pays premium to protect against a yield rise.
An interest rate option obliges the buyer to transact.
Basis risk in IRF
Hedging with futures leaves basis risk because the portfolio and the contract do not move together perfectly.
A hedge does not offset all loss because bonds differ.
A futures hedge removes every kind of risk.
Who uses IRDs
Banks, mutual funds, insurers and corporates use interest rate derivatives to manage rate risk.
A debt fund manager uses futures to manage duration.
Interest rate derivatives are only for speculators.

units.title: Strategies using interest rate derivatives and distributor conduct
units.overview: Hedging and trading strategies with interest rate derivatives and the distributor's duties for complex products.
facts: Hedging a bond portfolio
A holder of bonds fears a rise in yields and hedges by selling interest rate futures to offset the fall in bond values.
A fund sells G-Sec futures against its bond holdings.
A holder of bonds hedges by buying more bonds.
Adjusting duration
A manager can lengthen or shorten a portfolio's effective duration using interest rate futures without selling bonds.
A manager reduces duration using short futures.
Duration can be changed only by selling bonds.
Trading a view on rates
A trader expecting yields to fall buys interest rate futures and one expecting yields to rise sells them.
A trader buys futures before an expected rate cut.
A trader expecting a rate cut sells futures.
Disclosure of complexity
Distributors must explain the strategy, derivative use and risks of a SIF in plain language before the investor decides.
A distributor explains how short positions can lose money.
A distributor should only mention likely gains.
No assured returns
Distributors must not promise or imply guaranteed returns on mutual funds or SIFs.
A distributor refuses to state a fixed return for a SIF.
A distributor may promise 12% for a SIF.
Code of conduct
Distributors must act with honesty and care, avoid mis-selling, keep client information confidential and disclose commissions.
A distributor discloses the commission and gives true information.
The code allows exaggerated claims.
Mis-selling
Mis-selling is selling a product that does not suit the client or by giving misleading information, and it can lead to penalties.
A distributor sells a complex SIF to a client who needs regular liquidity.
Mis-selling happens only if the client loses money.
